title: Fourteen client sites, and nobody files a copy ticket
excerpt: A nine-person studio moved every client site onto Starter in one quarter. Clients edit their own pages now; the studio spends its hours on new work.
imageAlt: Two designers at Bellwood & Vane reviewing printed page layouts pinned to a studio wall
figureOneLabel: client sites moved in one quarter
figureThreeLabel: from kickoff to a launched site
quote: Our clients used to email us a sentence and wait two days. Now they change it themselves before lunch, and we see it in the next pull request.
content:
Bellwood & Vane builds marketing sites for software companies and medical practices across North Carolina. Nine people, one office above a bike shop on Glenwood Avenue, and until last year, a support queue that was mostly other people’s sentences.

“We would launch a site we were proud of, and then spend the next six months changing it one ticket at a time,” says Tessa Bellwood, who founded the studio in 2017. “A new headline. A new photo of the new hire. A button that had to say Book a visit instead of Book an appointment. Every one of them went through a developer.”

The quarter they moved everything

The studio already built every site in Laravel with its own set of Blade components. That made the move smaller than they expected. Each component got a YAML file listing its fields, the pages became lists of sections, and the clients got a login to the editor.

They moved fourteen sites between January and March, two of them in a single week. The longest one, a dental group with forty-one pages, took a developer six days. Most took two.

What the clients do now

Clients open their own site, click the thing they want to change, and type. Images come from the media library or an upload. When they are happy, they press Publish, and the change lands in the site’s repository as an ordinary commit that the studio reviews the next morning.

Copy-change tickets dropped by 91% in the first sixty days. The ones that remain are requests for something new: a section the site does not have yet, or a page with a different shape.

What the studio does with the time

The studio’s developers now spend most of their week on new work. They have built a library of thirty-two sections of their own, shared across every client, and a new site starts from that library rather than from a blank folder. Kickoff to launch for a ten-page site is now three days.

“We charge for the sections and the strategy now, not for typing,” Tessa says. “It is a better business, and honestly a better job.”

title: A four-person marketing team that ships its own landing pages
excerpt: Ironside makes punch-list software for general contractors. Its marketing team now launches a landing page a week without a single engineering ticket.
imageAlt: Ironside’s head of marketing at a standing desk by tall windows in the Boise office
figureThreeLabel: largest paint on the home page, down from 2.4 s
quote: Engineering built the sections once. Since then we have launched thirty-eight pages and they have not heard from us once.
content:
Ironside sells punch-list and closeout software to general contractors, mostly in the Mountain West. The company has 140 people and a marketing team of four, and its marketing site used to belong to engineering.

“Every landing page was a sprint ticket,” says Lena Marchetti, who joined as head of marketing in 2025. “We would plan a campaign for a trade show in Denver, write the page, and then wait for a slot. Sometimes the slot came after the show.”

Sections built once

Ironside’s front-end team spent two weeks turning the components they already had into Starter sections: a hero with a product screenshot, a feature row, a customer quote, a pricing table, and a closing band. Each one got fields for everything a marketer would want to change, and a few toggles for the parts that are optional.

Then they handed over the keys. The marketing team builds pages by stacking those sections and filling in the words. Engineering reviews the occasional new section and otherwise stays out of it.

A page a week

Last quarter the team launched thirty-eight landing pages: one per trade show, one per regional campaign, and a set for a new integration with a scheduling tool. None of them needed an engineering ticket. The average page went from brief to live in a day and a half.

The pages are also faster than the ones they replaced. Because every section is plain Blade and every image has its dimensions set, the home page’s largest paint dropped from 2.4 seconds to 0.9 seconds without anyone working on performance directly.

What they would tell another team

“Spend the time on the sections,” Lena says. “If the sections are right, the pages are easy. We had one bad week early on where we tried to make a section do too many things with too many toggles. We split it into two and the problem went away.”

title: Pantry hours that are right the same afternoon
excerpt: A food bank network with thirty-one pantry partners keeps hours, locations and volunteer shifts current on its own site, edited by the people who know them.
imageAlt: Stonebridge’s volunteer coordinator holding a tablet in the warehouse, shelves of canned goods behind him
figureOneLabel: pantry partners listed and kept current
figureTwoLabel: from an hours change to the live site, down from 9 days
figureThreeLabel: saved a year on outside web work
quote: When a pantry changes its hours on a Tuesday, the site says so by Tuesday afternoon. That used to take us more than a week.
content:
Stonebridge Food Network supplies thirty-one pantry partners across Allegheny County from a warehouse in the Strip District. Its website has one job that matters more than any other: telling people where they can get food this week, and when.

“Pantry hours change all the time,” says Tom Kowalski, who coordinates partners and volunteers. “A church pantry loses a volunteer and closes Thursdays. A school pantry adds a Saturday in the summer. If the website is wrong, a family takes two buses to a locked door.”

Nine days was too long

Before last year, the site was maintained by a freelance developer on a monthly retainer. Changes were batched and sent by email. The average time from a pantry calling with new hours to the site showing them was nine days.

A board member who builds Laravel apps for a living offered to rebuild the site on Starter over two weekends. The pantry list became a collection with a row per partner: name, address, hours, phone and a note. The pages that show it read from that one table.

Edited by the people who know

Tom and two other staff members now update the list themselves. When a pantry calls, they open the collection, change the row, and publish. The median time from the call to the live site is now four hours, and most changes are live the same afternoon.

The volunteer shift pages work the same way. When a Saturday sort needs twelve more people, the coordinator changes the number on the page and the call to sign up goes out the same day.

What it cost

The network ended the retainer and now spends nothing on outside web work in a normal month, about $11,400 a year. It runs on the Free plan for its single site, with the board member reviewing the occasional new section.

“We are not a tech organization,” Tom says. “We did not want to become one. This let us stay what we are and still have a website that tells the truth.”
